content: Stimming is a term used to describe a specific type of stereotypy, which refers to repetitive body movements that are often performed unconsciously. These movements are thought to self-stimulate one or more sensory systems in a controlled manner. The term stimming is shorthand for self-stimulation, and the behavior is hypothesized to serve a sensory-related function. Stereotypy is one of the diagnostic criteria for autism as outlined in the DSM-IV, but it is also observed in approximately 10% of neurotypical young children. It is important to note that not all individuals with autism exhibit stereotypy. Among those who do, common forms include hand flapping, spinning or rocking the body, lining up or spinning objects, echolalia (repeating words or phrases), perseveration (repeating actions or thoughts), and rote repetition of phrases. There are various theories regarding the purpose of stimming and why it is more prevalent in individuals with autism. For individuals who are hyposensitive, stimming may provide necessary stimulation to the nervous system, potentially releasing beta-endorphins. Conversely, for hypersensitive individuals, stimming may have a normalizing effect, allowing them to regulate a specific sensory input and providing a calming or soothing experience. In some cases, self-injurious behaviors are considered a form of stimming. While self-injury is generally distinct from stimming, individuals with reduced pain sensitivity may engage in self-injurious behaviors because they find the sensation pleasurable or stimulating, similar to other forms of stimming. For example, a person might enjoy the tactile sensation of biting their hand without perceiving the associated pain. Similarly, they might find the pressure on their forehead from head-banging to be satisfying, even if it does not cause them pain, despite the potential risk of serious injury such as brain damage.
